rationale: A wins because its best angles turn the launch into reportable tension without overclaiming: "Replit says anyone can build an app with plain English. It won't say how often those apps actually work." is a real accountability story with the missing proof named cleanly. B has good bones, especially the reliability angle, but it keeps stepping onto thin ice with lines like "ships a whole working app from one English sentence" and a pricing angle that admits "Without real numbers this is a topic, not a story." A is sharper, better bounded, and less willing to decorate gaps as angles.
gaps_in_A: "Who's checking what's in them?" is a legitimate security question, but the angle stretches into "inside organizations and schools" without any supplied fact that the agent is used in workplaces or that generated databases will hold sensitive third-party data.
"turn its tens of millions of users into app publishers overnight" is punchy but slightly inflated; the facts give platform reach, not agent adoption or publishing behavior.
The education angle is strong, but "Now it can write the homework too" edges toward columnist language; it needs a real educator/source before that framing can carry weight.
gaps_in_B: "from one English sentence" is not in the update. The fact is a plain-English description; one sentence is a cute compression that may be false.
"Replit is betting class on it" is garbled and overdramatic; the update says Replit is used heavily in education, not that classrooms are adopting the agent.
"which is most students before a course, not after" is an invented classroom claim. No student skill distribution was supplied.
The pricing angle says "You pay per build" and then admits it does not know whether the unit is "per build? per deploy? per token?" That is not rigor; that is the headline outrunning the facts.
